75238.q: What is the French original of the round known in English as “Are You Sleeping, Brother John?”?
75238.e: “Frère Jacques” is an old French children’s song. It has been translated into many languages and is sung as a round all over the world.
75238.m: “Brother John” comes from France, where it is called “Frère Jacques”.

75239.q: What do all the groups sing in a round?
a: The same melody, but starting at different times
All the same note at the same time
75239.e: In a round one group starts and the next ones come in later with the same melody. This creates several parts. A famous example of a canon is the one by Johann Pachelbel.
75239.m: In a round everyone sings the same melody one after another.

75240.q: What is the smallest number of groups needed for a round to sound in parts?
75240.e: Even with two groups starting at different times, two voices sound at once. Many rounds are written for three or four groups.
75240.m: A round needs at least two voices.

75241.q: How does the melody of “Brother John” sound when played in a minor key?
a: Exactly the same as in major
75241.e: Minor usually sounds darker than major. The composer Gustav Mahler even turned “Brother John” in minor into a funeral march in his 1st Symphony.
75241.m: In a minor key even a cheerful song sounds sad.

75242.q: What do you call a round that can start again from the beginning over and over?
75242.e: In a perpetual canon the end of the melody leads seamlessly back to the beginning. So it can be repeated as often as you like.
75242.m: A perpetual canon goes round and round like a wheel.

75243.q: Which Latin round asking for peace is often sung by choirs?
75243.e: “Dona nobis pacem” means “Give us peace”. This three-part round is widely sung in schools and choirs.
75243.m: “Dona nobis pacem” is a well-known round for peace.

75244.e: Johann Strauss II composed a great many waltzes in 19th-century Vienna. They made him world-famous.
75244.m: Johann Strauss II is the famous Waltz King.

75245.q: What is the best-known waltz by Johann Strauss II called?
75245.e: The Blue Danube waltz was written in 1867 and is seen as Austria’s unofficial anthem. It is played every year at the New Year’s Concert in Vienna.
75245.m: The Blue Danube is the most famous waltz from Vienna.

75246.q: Which waltz is the faster dance?
75246.e: The Viennese waltz is danced at about 60 bars per minute, the slow waltz at only about 30. That is why you turn much faster in the Viennese waltz.
75246.m: The Viennese waltz is much faster than the slow waltz.

75247.q: What is the slow waltz also called?
75247.e: The slow waltz developed in England. That is why it is also called the English waltz.
75247.m: The slow waltz is also called the English waltz.

75248.q: In which two cities on the Río de la Plata did the tango begin?
a: Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo
75248.e: The tango began at the end of the 19th century in the harbour districts of both cities. Many immigrants brought influences from Europe and Africa.
75248.m: The tango comes from the port cities on the Río de la Plata.

75249.q: Which bellows instrument shapes the sound of Argentine tango?
75249.e: The bandoneon was invented in Germany and reached South America with emigrants. There it became the typical tango instrument.
75249.m: The bandoneon is the heart of the tango.

75250.q: In which country is the tango seen as the typical national dance?
75250.e: The tango began in Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Especially in Argentina it is still a symbol of the country today.
75250.m: The tango is the typical dance of Argentina.

75251.q: What kind of dance is the tango?
75251.e: In the tango two people dance close together. One leads, the other follows.
75251.m: The tango is danced in pairs.

75252.e: The B stands for “break”, the part of a song people danced to. The dancers themselves often call their dance “breaking”.
75252.m: Breakdancers are called B-girls and B-boys.

75253.q: In which hip-hop dance style do you tense your muscles sharply so that your body seems to twitch?
75253.e: In popping, muscles are briefly tensed and released in time with the beat. This creates a robot-like, twitching effect.
75253.m: In popping the muscles twitch to the beat of the music.

75254.q: What is the breakdance move called in which you spin on your head?
75254.e: In a headspin the dancer balances on her head and spins like a top. Dancers often wear a hat or helmet for it.
75254.m: In a headspin you spin on your head.

75255.q: At which Olympic Games was breaking an Olympic event for the first time?
75255.e: Breaking made its Olympic debut at the 2024 Summer Games in Paris. It was not included in the programme for Los Angeles 2028.
75255.m: Breaking was Olympic for the first time in Paris in 2024.

75256.q: What do you call a small band that plays traditional Swiss dance music?
75256.e: A Ländler band often has a Schwyzerörgeli or accordion, clarinet, piano and double bass. It plays Ländler, schottische, polka and waltz.
75256.m: A Ländler band plays traditional Swiss dance music.

75257.q: What do you call a yodel sung entirely without words?
75257.e: In a Naturjodel you only sing syllables like “jo-ho-di”, but no text. A well-known example is the Appenzell Zäuerli.

75258.q: What is spun round in a clay bowl in the Appenzell Talerschwingen?
75258.e: In Talerschwingen a coin, usually a five-franc piece, is made to roll round and round in a clay bowl. This makes a long, humming sound that accompanies yodelling.
75258.m: In Talerschwingen a spinning coin sings in a bowl.

75259.q: What is the prayer call that alpine herdsmen call out through a milk funnel in the evening?
75259.e: With the Betruf, also called the alpine blessing, the herdsmen ask for protection for people and animals on the alp. The milk funnel amplifies the voice like a megaphone.
75259.m: The Betruf is an old blessing call on the alp.

75260.q: What is the big festival called where yodellers, alphorn players and flag throwers meet every three years?
75260.e: The Federal Yodelling Festival is organised by the Swiss Yodelling Association. It takes place every three years in a different region.
75260.m: The Federal Yodelling Festival takes place every three years.

75261.q: Which small accordion is typical of Swiss folk music?
75261.e: The Schwyzerörgeli is a small diatonic accordion. In many Ländler bands it plays the melody.
75261.m: The Schwyzerörgeli is the typical instrument of Ländler music.

75262.q: What are the large forged bells called that people shake in time during Trychle?
75262.e: Treicheln are forged from sheet metal and have a dull, loud sound. During Trychle, groups walk in step and swing them in rhythm.
75262.m: Treicheln are forged bells used in Swiss customs.

75263.q: What is an alphorn traditionally made of?
75263.e: The alphorn is usually made of spruce wood. Although it is made of wood, it counts as a brass instrument because of its mouthpiece.
75263.m: The alphorn is made of wood.

75264.q: What is the famous herding song from the canton of Fribourg that is sung at the Fête des Vignerons in Vevey?
75264.e: “Le Ranz des vaches” is a cow call in the Fribourg dialect. It recalls the herds being taken up to the alpine pastures.
75264.m: “Le Ranz des vaches” is a famous cow call from Fribourg.

75265.q: What is the subject called in which you learn music mainly through movement?
75265.e: In eurhythmics children experience beat and tempo with their whole body. It was invented by the Geneva music teacher Émile Jaques-Dalcroze.

75266.q: What do children often do to music in a eurhythmics lesson?
75266.e: In eurhythmics children walk, clap and jump to the music. That way they feel beat and tempo in their bodies.
75266.m: In eurhythmics you learn music through movement.

75267.q: Which way does the hand move on the first beat of a bar when conducting?
75267.e: The first beat is shown with a clear downward movement. That way everyone sees the start of the bar at once.
75267.m: When conducting, the first beat goes down.

75268.q: In 3/4 time, which way does a right-handed conductor move for the second beat?
75268.e: In 3/4 time the hand draws roughly a triangle. For the second beat it moves out to the right.
75268.m: In triple time the second beat goes to the right.

75269.q: Using Zoltán Kodály’s method, which rhythm syllable do you say for a crotchet (quarter note)?
75269.e: Kodály used simple syllables so that children can speak and clap rhythms. Two quavers are called “ti-ti”.
75269.m: Rhythm syllables help you speak and feel note values.

75270.q: By how much do two dots to the right of a note lengthen it?
a: By three quarters of its value
By a quarter of its value
75270.e: The first dot adds half the note’s value, the second adds half of that again, so a quarter. Together that makes a half plus a quarter, which is three quarters.
75270.m: A second dot adds half the value of the first dot.

75271.q: How many quavers (eighth notes) does a dotted crotchet last?
75271.e: A crotchet lasts two quavers. The dot adds half, so one quaver: 2 plus 1 makes 3 quavers.
75271.m: A dotted crotchet lasts as long as three quavers.

75272.q: A piece in 4/4 time lasts exactly 32 crotchet beats. How many bars does it have?
75272.e: Each bar of 4/4 contains four crotchet beats. 32 divided by 4 makes 8 bars.
75272.m: You get the number of bars by dividing all the beats by the beats per bar.

75273.q: In the treble clef, which note sits on the top line?
75273.e: The fourth line is D and the top space is E. So the top line above it is F, an octave above the F in the bottom space.
75273.m: The top line in the treble clef is F.

75274.q: In the treble clef, which note sits on the middle line?
75274.e: The third line is exactly in the middle of the stave. In the treble clef the B above middle C sits there.
75274.m: On the middle line of the treble clef sits B.

75275.q: Which group of clefs do the alto and tenor clefs belong to?
75275.e: The centre of the alto and tenor clefs points to the line of middle C. That is why they are called C clefs.
75275.m: The alto and tenor clefs are C clefs.

75276.q: In the bass clef, which note sits on the bottom line?
75276.e: Counting from the bottom in the bass clef, the first line is G and the second line is B.
75276.m: The bottom line in the bass clef is G.

75277.q: Which major key has two flats in its key signature?
75277.e: In B flat major the notes B and E are lowered to B flat and E flat. That is why there are two flats in the key signature.
75277.m: B flat major has the flats B flat and E flat.

75278.q: Which minor key shares its key signature with F major?
75278.e: The relative minor lies a minor third below the keynote of the major key. A minor third below F is D.
75278.m: D minor is the relative minor of F major.

75279.q: Which notes make up the G major triad?
75279.e: Above G, B forms a major third, and above that D forms a minor third. That makes a major triad.
75279.m: The G major triad is made of G, B and D.

75280.q: Which major key, like A minor, has no sharps or flats at all?
75280.e: A minor is the relative minor of C major. Both use only the white keys of the piano and so have no sharps or flats.
75280.m: A minor is the relative minor of C major.

75281.q: What does “subito piano” mean in written music?
75281.e: Subito is Italian for “at once, suddenly”. So the volume changes to quiet without any transition.
75281.m: Subito means that something happens suddenly.

75282.q: What does “decrescendo” mean in written music?
75282.e: Decrescendo means “decreasing” in Italian. The volume falls bit by bit. The opposite is crescendo.

75283.q: What is the dynamic level between piano and mezzo forte called?
75283.e: From quiet to loud the levels are pp, p, mp, mf, f and ff. So mezzo piano (mp) is a little louder than piano.
75283.m: Mezzo piano is a little louder than piano.

75284.q: What does the tempo marking “Moderato” mean?
75284.e: Moderato comes from the Italian word for “moderate”. The tempo is neither slow nor fast.

75285.q: What does the performance marking “rubato” mean?
a: Shaping the tempo freely, with slight changes
Keeping the tempo exactly the same
75285.e: Rubato means “stolen”: you take a little time here and give it back there. It is typical of Romantic piano music.
75285.m: In rubato the tempo can breathe freely.

75286.q: What does the tempo marking “Vivace” mean?
75286.e: Vivace means “lively” in Italian. The tempo is quick and cheerful.

75287.q: What does the tempo marking “Lento” mean?
75287.e: Lento is Italian for “slow”. It is one of the calmest tempo markings.

75288.q: What is the tempo marking for “as fast as possible”, even faster than presto?
75288.e: The ending -issimo means “very” or “most”. So prestissimo is the fastest usual tempo.
75288.m: The ending -issimo makes a tempo marking stronger.

75289.q: What does the tempo marking “Grave” mean?
75289.e: Grave is Italian for “heavy, serious”. It stands for a very slow, weighty tempo.
75289.m: Grave means heavy and very slow.

75290.q: What is the very low female voice, below the normal alto, called?
75290.e: The contralto is the lowest female voice. This voice type is rare.
75290.m: The contralto is the lowest female voice.

75291.q: What is the male voice between baritone and deep bass called?
75291.e: The bass-baritone combines the depth of the bass with the height of the baritone. In opera it often sings roles like Wotan in Wagner.
75291.m: The bass-baritone lies between baritone and bass.

75292.q: What do you call imitating drum sounds using only your mouth, lips and voice?
75292.e: In beatboxing you make bass, snare and hi-hat sounds with your mouth alone. It is an important art form of hip-hop culture.
75292.m: In beatboxing your mouth becomes a drum kit.

75293.q: Which way does the hand move on the last beat of a bar when conducting?
75293.e: The last beat goes up so that the hand can swing back for the next first beat. That is why it is also called the upbeat.
75293.m: When conducting, the last beat of a bar goes up.

75394.q: According to the colour theory you learn at school, how many primary colours are there in the paint box?
75394.e: At school you learn about three primary colours. You can mix many other colours from them.

75395.q: Which colour is a primary colour?
75395.e: Yellow is one of the three primary colours. Green, orange and purple only come about through mixing.

75396.q: Which of these colours is also a primary colour?
75396.e: Blue is a primary colour. Brown, pink and grey are mixed colours.

75397.q: Which primary colour is in both orange and purple?
75397.e: Orange contains red and yellow, and purple contains red and blue. What they both have is red.
75397.m: Red is in orange and in purple.

75398.q: Can you mix a primary colour from other paints?
75398.e: Primary colours cannot be mixed from other colours. That is why they are called primary colours.
75398.m: You cannot mix a primary colour.

75399.q: Which Swiss artist developed a famous colour theory with a colour wheel?
75399.e: Johannes Itten was born in the canton of Bern in 1888. He taught at the Bauhaus in Germany and wrote a well-known book about colours.
75399.m: Johannes Itten was a Swiss colour theorist.

75400.q: Which primary colour do you need for both green and orange?
75400.e: For green you mix yellow with blue, and for orange yellow with red. So both contain yellow.
75400.m: Yellow is in green and in orange.

75401.q: What happens to watercolour paint when you add a lot of water?
75401.e: A lot of water thins the paint. The white paper shows through and the colour looks light.
75401.m: With a lot of water, paint becomes lighter.

75402.q: What kind of green do you get when you mix a lot of yellow with only a little blue?
75402.e: The more yellow there is in the mixture, the lighter and more yellowish the green becomes.
75402.m: With more yellow, green becomes lighter.

75403.q: Which colour do you get from blue and a lot of white?
75403.e: White lightens any colour. So blue becomes a light blue like the sky.
75403.m: White turns blue into light blue.

75404.q: Which colour do you get from red and a little black?
75404.e: Even a little black makes red much darker.
75404.m: Red with black becomes dark red.

75405.q: What is the best colour to start with if you want to mix a light colour?
75405.e: You add the dark colour to the light one in small amounts. The other way round, you need a great deal of paint.
75405.m: Add a little dark to the light colour.

75406.q: Which colour do you get from black and white?
75406.e: Black and white together make grey. The more white, the lighter the grey.

75407.q: What do you usually get when you mix all three primary colours together?
75407.e: If you mix red, yellow and blue, the colour becomes dark and brownish.
75407.m: All the primary colours together become dark and brown.

75408.q: What are colours that you mix from two primary colours called?
75408.e: Green, orange and purple come from two primary colours. They are called secondary colours.
75408.m: Secondary colours come from primary colours.

75409.q: Which season is often painted with cool colours?
75409.e: In winter there is snow and ice. Blue, turquoise and white suit it.
75409.m: Winter is often painted with cool colours.

75410.q: Which group does the colour turquoise belong to?
75410.e: Turquoise lies between blue and green. It looks fresh like sea water.

75411.q: Which colour is considered a cool colour?
75411.e: Blue reminds us of ice and cold water. That is why it counts as a cool colour.

75412.q: What do warm colours often remind us of?
75412.e: Red, orange and yellow look like fire and the sun. That is why they seem warm.
75412.m: Warm colours remind us of fire.

75413.q: What do cool colours often remind us of?
75413.e: Blue and turquoise look like ice and water. That is why they seem cool.
75413.m: Cool colours remind us of ice and water.

75414.q: Which colours are best for painting a crackling campfire?
75414.e: Warm colours suit fire. They glow and look hot.
75414.m: You paint fire with warm colours.

75415.q: Which colours are best for painting a glacier in winter?
75415.e: A glacier is cold. That is why cool colours such as blue and turquoise suit it.
75415.m: You paint ice with cool colours.

75417.q: How does a room painted entirely in red and orange often feel?
75417.e: Red and orange are warm colours. They make a room feel warm.
75417.m: Warm colours make a room cosy.

75418.q: What does a colour wheel show?
75418.e: On the colour wheel, the colours are arranged round in a circle. This shows which colours are related.
75418.m: The colour wheel puts the colours in order.

75419.q: How many colours does Johannes Itten's well-known colour wheel have?
75419.e: Itten's colour wheel has twelve colour fields. They include primary colours, secondary colours and in-between shades.
75419.m: Itten's colour wheel has twelve colours.

75420.q: Which shape do the three primary colours form in the middle of Itten's colour wheel?
75420.e: In the middle of Itten's colour wheel there is a triangle. It is divided into three fields with the three primary colours.
75420.m: In Itten's colour wheel, the primary colours are in a triangle.

75421.q: What are colours that sit right next to each other on the colour wheel called?
75421.e: Neighbouring colours such as yellow and orange sit side by side on the colour wheel. Together they look harmonious and calm.
75421.m: Neighbouring colours sit next to each other on the colour wheel.

75422.q: Which colour is opposite yellow on the colour wheel?
75422.e: Yellow and purple are a pair of opposite colours. They are also called complementary colours.
75422.m: Yellow and purple are opposite colours.

75423.q: What are two colours that face each other on the colour wheel called?
75423.e: Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel are called complementary colours. They are also called opposite colours.

75424.q: Where is orange on the colour wheel?
75424.e: A secondary colour sits on the colour wheel between the colours it is made from.
75424.m: Secondary colours sit between their primary colours.

75425.q: How do two opposite colours look when you paint them next to each other?
75425.e: Opposite colours strengthen each other. That is why they stand out especially next to each other.
75425.m: Opposite colours look very bright next to each other.

75426.q: How does watercolour paint usually change when it dries?
75426.e: Wet paint shines and looks stronger. As it dries, it becomes a little lighter.

75427.q: What should you do before you take a new colour?
75427.e: With a clean brush, the new colour stays nice and clear. Otherwise it gets muddy.
75427.m: Wash out the brush before every new colour.

75428.q: What happens when you paint a lot of water onto the paper?
75428.e: Thin paper soaks up the water and goes wavy. Thick painting paper helps prevent this.
75428.m: Too much water makes paper go wavy.

75429.q: What is the metal part of a paintbrush that holds the hairs in place called?
75429.e: The ferrule is the little metal tube on the brush. It holds the hairs together.
75429.m: The ferrule holds the brush hairs in place.

75430.q: Which brush is good for thin, fine lines?
75430.e: A thin round brush has a fine tip. With it you can paint narrow lines.
75430.m: For fine lines you use a thin brush.

75431.q: What are watercolour paints that look see-through and let the paper show through called?
75431.e: The German word Aquarell comes from the Latin word for water. These paints are thin and translucent.

75432.q: What do you need a cloth for when painting with watercolours?
75432.e: You use the cloth to dab extra water out of the brush.

75433.q: What happens when you dab watercolour paint onto wet paper?
a: It rolls off the paper in drops
75433.e: On wet paper, the paint flows apart softly. This creates soft blends.
75433.m: On wet paper, the paint spreads out.

75434.q: What are wax crayons mainly made of?
75434.e: Wax crayons are made of wax with colour powder mixed into it.
75434.m: Wax crayons are made of wax.

75435.q: What happens to wax crayons when they lie in the hot sun?
75435.e: Wax melts when it is warm. That is why the crayons go soft and can melt.
75435.m: Wax goes soft in the heat.

75436.q: How do you colour a large area quickly with a wax crayon?
a: With the long side of the crayon
75436.e: You take the paper off the crayon and colour with its side. That way the area quickly becomes colourful.
75436.m: You colour large areas with the side of the crayon.

75437.q: You put paper on a leaf and rub over it with a wax crayon. What do you see?
a: A mirror image of the leaf
75437.e: A leaf has fine veins. Rubbing makes them visible on the paper. This technique is called frottage.

75438.q: What happens when you paint over a wax drawing with watercolour?
75438.e: Wax and water do not get on. The watercolour runs off the wax in drops and the drawing stays visible.

75439.q: What do you use to draw a “secret picture” that only appears when you paint over it with watercolour?
75439.e: You can hardly see white wax on white paper. When you paint over it with colour, the picture appears.
75439.m: White wax becomes visible with paint.

75440.q: How do you make a scratch picture with wax crayons?
a: Paint black over a colourful layer, then scratch
Wipe a picture away with water
Tear up paper and glue it
75440.e: First you colour everything brightly, then paint black over the top. When you scratch, the bright colours come through again.
75440.m: In a scratch picture, you scratch the colour free.

75441.q: Why are wax crayons good for small children?
a: They are thick and rarely break
They are as sharp as needles
75441.e: Wax crayons are thick and sturdy. Small hands can hold them well.
75441.m: Wax crayons fit well in small hands.

75442.q: What do you do to paper to give it soft, uneven edges for a collage?
75442.e: Torn paper has a soft, frayed edge. Cut paper has smooth edges.

75443.q: Which language does the word “collage” come from?
75443.e: The French word “coller” means to glue.

75444.q: Which tools do you need most for a collage?
75444.e: You cut out the pieces with the scissors. You stick them on with the glue.
75444.m: For a collage you need scissors and glue.

75445.q: Which material is good for a collage?
75445.e: You can cut pictures and letters out of magazines and stick them on.
75445.m: Old magazines are good collage material.

75446.q: Which famous painter made the first collages together with Georges Braque?
75446.e: Around 1912, Picasso and Braque glued pieces of paper into their pictures. That is how collage became known in art.
75446.m: Picasso was gluing collages early on.

75447.q: Which French artist, in old age, cut colourful shapes out of paper with scissors?
75447.e: Henri Matisse was ill and could hardly paint any more. So he cut out coloured paper shapes and stuck them on.
75447.m: In old age, Matisse painted with scissors.

75448.q: What is the old Swiss art of cutting delicate pictures out of paper called?
75448.e: Paper cutting is especially famous in the Pays-d'Enhaut in the canton of Vaud. It often shows cows being taken up to the Alpine pastures.
75448.m: Paper cutting is a Swiss folk art.

75449.q: Which natural material can you collect in autumn for a collage?
75449.e: In autumn the leaves are red, yellow and brown. Once dried, they are easy to stick on.
75449.m: Autumn leaves are good for collages.

75450.q: What do people often use to make a simple stamp print at school?
75450.e: You cut a pattern into half a potato. Then you put paint on it and press it onto the paper.
75450.m: A potato can be a stamp.

75451.q: How does a letter appear on the paper if it is the right way round on the stamp?
75451.e: When you print, everything is mirrored. That is why you have to cut letters into the stamp back to front.
75451.m: A print is back to front.

75452.q: What do you need a roller for when printing?
75452.e: With the roller you roll the paint thinly and evenly onto the printing block.

75453.q: In lino printing, what do you use to cut the grooves into the soft block?
75453.e: You use a small gouge to cut grooves into the soft linoleum. These parts stay white when you print.
75453.m: In lino printing, you cut with a gouge.

75454.q: Which parts of a potato stamp print colour onto the paper?
75454.e: Only what sticks up touches the paper. The parts cut away stay white.
75454.m: On a stamp, only what sticks up prints.

75455.q: What can you cover with paint and print to show fine veins?
75455.e: You paint a leaf and press it onto the paper. The veins then appear as a fine pattern.
75455.m: A leaf leaves a beautiful print.

75456.q: What must you put on the stamp before every new print?
75456.e: When printing, the stamp passes its paint to the paper. For the next print it needs paint again.
75456.m: Before every print, put new paint on the stamp.

75457.q: How many identical pictures can you print with a monotype?
75457.e: “Mono” means one. A monotype produces just a single print.

75458.q: Which shape has no corners at all?
75458.e: A circle curves all the way round. That is why it has no corners.

75459.q: Which shape has four sides of the same length and four right angles?
75459.e: In a square, all four sides are the same length.
75459.m: A square has four equal sides.

75460.q: What is a line that goes up and down like pointed mountains called?
75460.e: A zigzag line has sharp corners. A wavy line, on the other hand, is soft and round.
75460.m: A zigzag line has sharp points.

75461.q: What is a line that turns inwards like a snail's shell called?
75461.e: A spiral keeps turning around a centre point.

75462.q: What is a line that goes from top to bottom like a flagpole called?
75462.e: A vertical line stands straight up. A horizontal line lies flat like the horizon.
75462.m: Vertical means from top to bottom.

75463.q: Which painter from Russia liked to paint circles, triangles and lines?
75463.e: Wassily Kandinsky is considered a pioneer of abstract art. His pictures often show colourful shapes instead of things.
75463.m: Kandinsky painted with shapes and colours.

75464.q: What is a line made up of lots of little dots called?
75464.e: If you put lots of dots one after another, you get a dotted line.
75464.m: A dotted line is made of dots.

75465.q: What is a picture showing the face of another person called?
75465.e: A portrait shows a person, often only the head and shoulders. If you paint yourself, it becomes a self-portrait.

75466.q: In the past, what did a painter usually need in order to paint a self-portrait?
75466.e: In the mirror, painters see their own face. That way they can copy it.
75466.m: For a self-portrait, you look in the mirror.

75467.q: What is a self-portrait taken with a mobile phone called?
75467.e: A selfie is a photo of yourself. It is a modern form of self-portrait.
75467.m: A selfie is a photo of yourself.

75468.q: Roughly where are the eyes in a drawn face?
a: In the middle of the head
Right at the top of the head
Right at the bottom by the chin
75468.e: Many people think the eyes are high up. In reality, they are at about half the height of the head.
75468.m: The eyes are about halfway down the head.

75469.q: Roughly where are the ears in a drawn face?
a: Between the eyes and the tip of the nose
75469.e: The ears begin at about the height of the eyes and eyebrows. They end at about the height of the tip of the nose.
75469.m: The ears reach from the eyes to the nose.

75470.q: Which painter with a red beard often painted himself, including in a straw hat?
75470.e: Vincent van Gogh had little money for models. That is why he often painted himself.

75471.q: What is different in a mirror compared with reality?
75471.e: In the mirror, your right hand appears as your left hand. That is why self-portraits often show a mirrored face.
75471.m: A mirror swaps left and right.

75472.q: Which German artist painted himself from the front with long curls in 1500?
75472.e: Albrecht Dürer from Nuremberg painted several self-portraits. The picture from 1500 is especially famous.

75473.e: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa in Italy more than 500 years ago.
75473.m: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa.

75474.q: What colours is the headscarf in Vermeer's “Girl with a Pearl Earring”?
75474.e: The girl wears a blue turban with a yellow cloth. Jan Vermeer was a painter from Holland.
75474.m: Vermeer's girl wears a blue and yellow cloth.

75475.q: What is the “Mona Lisa” especially known for?
75475.e: Many people puzzle over whether the Mona Lisa is smiling or not.

75476.q: What shines in the sky in Vincent van Gogh's painting “The Starry Night”?
75476.e: Van Gogh painted a night sky with swirling, shining stars and a bright moon.
75476.m: Stars and the moon shine in The Starry Night.

75478.q: Where did Michelangelo paint his famous pictures in the Sistine Chapel in Rome?
75478.e: For years, Michelangelo painted high up on scaffolding on the chapel ceiling.

75479.q: What does Edvard Munch's painting “The Scream” show?
a: A figure with its hands on its face
75479.e: The figure holds its hands to its head and has its mouth wide open.
75479.m: The Scream shows a frightened figure.

75480.q: Which mountain can be seen small in the background of Hokusai's picture “The Great Wave”?
75480.e: Behind the huge wave you can see Mount Fuji, small. It is the highest mountain in Japan.
75480.m: Mount Fuji stands behind the Great Wave.

75481.q: Which painter liked to paint mountains, cows and mountain farmers in the Engadine?
75481.e: Giovanni Segantini spent his last years in Maloja in the Engadine. There is a museum with his paintings in St Moritz.
75481.m: Segantini painted life in the Alps.

75482.q: What did Henri Rousseau often paint, even though he had never been there?
75482.e: Henri Rousseau got his ideas from the botanical garden and zoo in Paris. His jungle pictures are full of leaves and animals.
75482.m: Rousseau painted jungles from his imagination.

75483.q: In which village in the canton of Bern was Albert Anker born?
75483.e: Albert Anker was born in Ins in the Seeland. He also died there.

75484.q: In which century did Albert Anker mainly live?
75484.e: Albert Anker lived from 1831 to 1910. That is mainly the 19th century.
75484.m: Albert Anker lived in the 19th century.

75485.q: Who did Albert Anker especially like to paint, and paint often?
75485.e: Albert Anker painted many pictures of children reading, knitting, playing or sleeping.

75486.q: What was Albert Anker supposed to become before he became a painter?
75486.e: Anker was first supposed to become a priest and studied at university for this. Then he decided on art.
75486.m: Anker first wanted to become a priest.

75487.q: Which country did the painter Albert Anker come from?
75487.e: Albert Anker was born in Ins in the canton of Bern. He is one of the best-known painters in Switzerland.
75487.m: Albert Anker was a Swiss painter.

75488.q: Which place often appears in Albert Anker's paintings?
75488.e: Anker painted several pictures of classrooms and school exams, for example “The School Examination”.
75488.m: Anker often painted the village school.

75489.q: Albert Anker did not only paint on canvas. What else did he paint many pictures on?
75489.e: Anker painted many ceramic plates and dishes for a workshop in Paris.

75490.q: What can you visit in Ins today to see where Anker worked?
75490.e: The Anker House in Ins shows his studio just as he used it.
75490.m: The Anker House is in Ins.

75491.q: What did Albert Anker do for a few years alongside painting?
a: He was a politician in Bern
He was a cook in Paris
75491.e: From 1870 to 1874, Albert Anker sat in the Grand Council of the canton of Bern. There he worked for art and schools.
75491.m: Anker was also a politician in the canton of Bern.

75492.q: In the six-part colour wheel, what kind of colour is the complementary colour of a secondary colour always?
75492.e: A secondary colour such as orange is made from two primary colours. Opposite it is always the third primary colour, the one not involved, so for orange it is blue.
75492.m: The complementary colour of a secondary colour is always a primary colour.

75493.q: How many complementary pairs are there in a six-part colour wheel with three primary and three secondary colours?
75493.e: Each of the three primary colours has exactly one secondary colour opposite it. So six colours form three pairs.
75493.m: The six-part colour wheel has three complementary pairs.

75494.q: What do you usually get when you mix two complementary colours from the paint box in equal parts?
75494.e: When mixing paints (subtractive mixing), complementary colours cancel each other out. The result is a muted, dull shade.
75494.m: If you mix complementary colours, the colour turns dull and greyish.

75495.q: What effect do complementary colours have when they are placed right next to each other?
a: They make each other look brighter
They both look paler and duller
They merge into a single colour
They become invisible to the eye
75495.e: When complementary colours are side by side, they boost each other's brightness. This is called complementary contrast.
75495.m: Complementary colours side by side look especially bright.

75496.q: Which complementary colour do you see as an afterimage if you stare at a red dot for a long time and then look at a white sheet of paper?
75496.e: The eye gets tired of red and then produces an afterimage in the opposite colour. This afterimage looks greenish.
75496.m: An afterimage appears in the complementary colour.

75497.q: How many colours does the well-known colour wheel of the Swiss artist Johannes Itten have?
75497.e: Itten's colour wheel consists of 3 primary colours, 3 secondary colours and 6 tertiary colours. It is still used in schools today.
75497.m: Johannes Itten created a twelve-part colour wheel.

75498.q: Which pair of colours is a complementary pair?
75498.e: Red is opposite green on the colour wheel. The other pairs sit right next to each other on the colour wheel.
75498.m: Red and green are complementary colours.

75499.q: What are colours such as orange, green and purple, which are mixed from two primary colours, called?
75499.e: Secondary colours come from two primary colours. If you mix a secondary colour with another colour, you get tertiary colours.
75499.m: You mix a secondary colour from two primary colours.

75500.q: In a perspective drawing, what is the point where parallel lines meet called?
75500.e: In perspective, parallel lines leading into the distance seem to meet at one point. This point is called the vanishing point.
75500.m: Parallel lines leading into the distance meet at the vanishing point.

75501.q: On which line do the vanishing points lie in a drawing where you look straight ahead?
a: On the bottom edge of the picture
On the diagonal of the picture
75501.e: The horizon line shows the viewer's eye level. When you look straight ahead, all the vanishing points lie on this line.
75501.m: The vanishing points lie on the horizon.

75502.q: How many vanishing points does two-point perspective have when you draw a house from its corner?
75502.e: In two-point perspective you see two sides of a building. The edges of each side run towards their own vanishing point, so there are two.
75502.m: Two-point perspective has two vanishing points.

75503.q: What is the view from far below looking up, which makes things look especially big and powerful, called?
75503.e: In a worm's-eye view, you look up from the ground. This makes people and buildings look huge.
75503.m: Seen from below in a worm's-eye view, things look powerful.

75504.q: What is the view from high above looking down on a landscape or a town called?
75504.e: A bird's-eye view shows a scene from above, the way a bird sees it while flying. You get a good overview.
75504.m: Seen from above, you look at the world from a bird's-eye view.

75505.q: What happens to the horizon line in a picture when the viewer climbs a ladder?
a: It moves up in the picture
It moves down in the picture
It disappears from the picture completely
75505.e: The horizon is always at the viewer's eye level. If you climb higher, the horizon rises in the picture too, and you see more of the ground.
75505.m: The horizon is always at eye level.

75506.q: In which era was linear perspective developed in Italy?
75506.e: Around 1420, the Florentine architect Filippo Brunelleschi showed how to draw spaces in correct perspective. Since then, artists have painted spaces with vanishing points.
75506.m: Linear perspective began in the Renaissance.

75507.q: How many vanishing points do you need to draw a tower block seen from below at an angle, with its vertical edges coming together?
75507.e: In three-point perspective, a third vanishing point above or below is added to the two on the horizon. This makes the vertical edges come together as well.
75507.m: Three-point perspective has three vanishing points.

75508.q: What is the part of a picture that seems closest to the viewer called?
75508.e: The foreground is right at the front of the picture, usually in the lower part. Behind it come the middle ground and the background.
75508.m: The foreground is right at the front of the picture.

75509.q: What is the area between the foreground and the background of a picture called?
75509.e: Many landscape paintings are divided into three zones. Between the foreground and the background lies the middle ground.
75509.m: The middle ground lies between front and back.

75510.q: Which technique shows most clearly in a picture that one object is in front of another?
a: It partly covers the other one
It is right in the middle
75510.e: When one object partly hides another, the eye immediately sees which one is in front. This overlapping creates a sense of space.
75510.m: Whatever covers something else is further forward.

75511.q: How do trees of the same size look in a picture when they are further away?
75511.e: The further away something is, the smaller it looks. Making things smaller like this creates depth in a picture.

75512.q: What does a trompe-l'œil painting, such as a painted window on the wall of a house, aim to do to the viewer?
75512.e: “Trompe-l'œil” is French and means “deceive the eye”. Such paintings look so real that people think they are real.

75513.q: How are objects in the background often drawn to give the picture depth?
75513.e: In the distance, the eye sees fewer details. That is why the background is painted more simply, while lots of details can be seen at the front.
75513.m: Show less detail in the background.

75514.q: Where are more distant things usually placed in a landscape picture without perspective lines?
a: Higher up, closer to the horizon
Lower down, at the bottom edge
Always right at the left edge
75514.e: The further away something stands on the ground, the closer it moves to the horizon line. That is why distant things are higher up in the picture.
75514.m: Distant things move up in the picture.

75515.q: In a photograph, what effect does a blurred background behind a sharply focused face have?
a: It makes the face stand out
It makes the picture look flatter
75515.e: A blurred background draws the eye to the sharp subject in the foreground. At the same time it creates a feeling of depth.
75515.m: A blurred background makes the main subject stand out.

75516.q: Why do painters use strong contrasts of light and dark?
a: So that the picture dries faster
So that less paint is needed
So that the picture looks flat
75516.e: Light and dark areas side by side make bodies look rounded and solid. The Italian technical term for this is chiaroscuro, meaning light and dark.
75516.m: Contrasts of light and dark make bodies look three-dimensional.

75517.q: What is the shadow that an object throws onto the ground or a wall called?
75517.e: A cast shadow falls away from the object onto another surface. A form shadow, by contrast, lies on the side of the object itself that faces away from the light.
75517.m: A cast shadow falls on another surface.

75518.q: What is the shadow on the side of an object itself that faces away from the light called?
75518.e: The form shadow appears on the object where no light falls. It makes a ball or a cube look three-dimensional.
75518.m: The form shadow lies on the object itself.

75519.q: What is showing shadow with lots of parallel lines called?
75519.e: For hatching, you draw lines lying close together. The closer the lines, the darker the area looks.
75519.m: With hatching, you draw shadows out of lines.

75520.q: How do you make pencil hatching darker without pressing harder?
a: You add lines crossways over the top
You draw the lines further apart
You partly rub the lines out again
75520.e: In cross-hatching, you add a second layer of lines across the first. This makes the area much darker.

75521.q: On which side of an apple is the cast shadow if the light comes from the top left?
a: To the right of the apple
To the left of the apple
In front of the apple at the top
75521.e: The shadow always falls on the side facing away from the light. If the light comes from the left, the shadow is on the right.
75521.m: The shadow always falls away from the light source.

75522.q: What is a row of boxes shaded evenly from white through greys to black called?
75522.e: A grey scale shows the steps between light and dark. It helps you draw shading carefully and finely.
75522.m: A grey scale shows the steps from white to black.

75523.q: Which Dutch painter, like Caravaggio, became famous for his special light in the dark and painted many self-portraits?
75523.e: Rembrandt made his figures stand out brightly from dark rooms. He painted himself dozens of times at every age.
75523.m: Rembrandt was a master of light and shadow.

75524.q: What property do watercolours have on paper?
75524.e: Watercolours form a thin layer of colour through which the paper shows. This makes the pictures look light and glowing.
75524.m: Watercolours let the paper show through.

75525.q: In classic watercolour painting, how do you get the brightest white areas?
75525.e: In watercolour, white is traditionally not painted. The white areas come from leaving the paper unpainted there.
75525.m: In watercolour, the paper is the white.

75526.q: What is the technique of painting watercolour onto paper that is still wet, so that it spreads softly, called?
75526.e: With wet-on-wet, the colours flow into each other and form soft blends. It is used for skies and clouds, for example.

75527.q: In which order do you usually work when painting with watercolours?
a: From the edge to the middle
75527.e: Because watercolours are translucent, you cannot paint light over dark. So you start with light shades and add dark ones last.
75527.m: In watercolour, you paint from light to dark.

75528.q: Which paper is best for watercolour painting?
75528.e: Watercolour paper is thick and absorbent so that it hardly goes wavy with lots of water. Thin paper would warp or tear.
75528.m: For watercolours you need thick paper.

75529.q: What is painting thin, translucent layers of colour on top of each other after they have dried called?
75529.e: When glazing, you put a transparent layer over a dried one. The colours mix visually on the paper.
75529.m: When glazing, you put thin layers of colour on top of each other.

75530.q: Which water-based paint, unlike watercolour, is opaque?
75530.e: Gouache contains more pigment and filler, so it covers. With it you can also paint light over dark.
75530.m: Gouache covers, watercolour lets the paper show through.

75531.q: Which printing process does linocut belong to?
75531.e: In a linocut, only the raised surface that is left prints. This is called relief printing, as with a woodcut or a stamp.
75531.m: Linocut is a relief printing process.

75532.q: Which parts stay white on the print in a linocut?
75532.e: The roller only puts ink on the raised surfaces. What you have cut away gets no ink and stays white.
75532.m: What you cut away stays white in the print.

75533.q: How does writing appear on the print if you cut it into the lino block so it reads normally?
75533.e: When printing, the image on the block is mirrored. That is why writing has to be cut into the block back to front.
75533.m: A print is the mirror image of the printing block.

75534.q: Which tool do you use to apply printing ink evenly to the lino block?
75534.e: The rubber roller spreads the ink thinly and evenly on the raised parts. That way no ink gets into the grooves.
75534.m: You apply printing ink with the roller.

75535.q: What are the tools with differently shaped blades used to cut lino called?
75535.e: Lino cutters are gouges with V-shaped or U-shaped blades. You use them to cut out fine lines or large areas.

75536.q: When cutting lino, where must you keep the hand that holds the block steady?
a: Directly in front of the blade
75536.e: If the sharp blade slips, it carries on in the cutting direction. That is why you always keep your other hand behind the blade, often using a bench hook.
75536.m: When cutting lino, keep your hand behind the blade.

75537.q: What is the method called in which, for a multicoloured linocut, you cut away more of the same block after each colour?
75537.e: In a reduction print, you print the lightest colour first and then carry on cutting. At the end the original block is used up, which is why the German name means “lost form”.
75537.m: In a reduction print, the block is cut away bit by bit.

75538.q: What is the dark room or box with a small hole through which an upside-down image appears called?
75538.e: In a camera obscura, light falls through a small hole and creates an upside-down image on the back wall. It is the forerunner of the camera.
75538.m: The camera obscura is the earliest form of the camera.

75539.q: How long did the oldest surviving photograph, from around 1826, need to be exposed?
75539.e: The Frenchman Joseph Nicéphore Niépce exposed a plate for hours to capture the view from his window. Today a photo takes only a fraction of a second.
75539.m: The first photos needed hours of exposure.

75540.q: What is the part of the lens called that controls how much light gets into the camera?
75540.e: The aperture is an adjustable opening in the lens. The wider it is open, the more light reaches the image sensor.
75540.m: The aperture controls the amount of light.

75541.q: Which lens brings faraway things close, like a telescope?
75541.e: A telephoto lens has a long focal length and magnifies distant subjects. A wide-angle lens, on the other hand, shows a large section of the scene.
75541.m: A telephoto lens brings distant things close.

75542.q: If you photograph a person with the sun behind them, what often appears as just a dark outline?
75542.e: With backlight, the background is much brighter than the person. The camera then shows the person as a dark silhouette.
75542.m: Backlight turns people into dark silhouettes.

75543.q: What does a camera's shutter speed affect most visibly?
a: Whether movement looks sharp or blurred
Whether the picture is colour or black and white
Whether the picture is portrait or landscape
How many pixels the picture has
75543.e: With a short exposure, movement is frozen. With a long exposure, moving things blur, such as flowing water.
75543.m: A long exposure makes movement blur.

75544.q: What is the area in front of and behind the subject that still looks sharp in a photo called?
75544.e: The depth of field decides how far the sharp area reaches. A wide-open aperture makes it small, so the background goes blurry.
75544.m: Depth of field shows how much of the picture is sharp.

75545.q: What is the composition rule called where you divide the picture into nine fields with two horizontal and two vertical lines?
75545.e: With the rule of thirds, you place the main subject on one of the lines or where they cross. This usually looks more exciting than a subject right in the middle.
75545.m: The rule of thirds puts the subject on a third line.

75546.q: How does a picture usually look when the main subject is exactly in the middle?
a: Calm, but often not very exciting
75546.e: A subject placed in the centre looks symmetrical and static. For more tension, people often place it a little off centre.
75546.m: A subject in the middle looks calm but often not very exciting.

75547.q: What are lines in a picture called, like a road or a fence, that lead the eye to the main subject?
75547.e: Leading lines guide the viewer's eye through the picture. Often they lead into the distance and so also create a sense of depth.
75547.m: Leading lines guide the eye to the subject.

75548.q: Which picture format do people usually choose for a portrait of a single person?
75548.e: A standing person is taller than they are wide. Portrait format therefore suits portraits, while landscapes are often shown in landscape format.
75548.m: Portraits are usually taken in portrait format.

75549.q: What effect do slanting, diagonal lines have in a picture?
a: They look dynamic and full of movement
They make the picture look empty
75549.e: Diagonals bring movement and tension into a picture. Horizontal lines, on the other hand, look calm and balanced.
75549.m: Diagonals bring movement into a picture.

75550.q: In which direction should a person in a picture usually have more free space?
a: In the direction they are looking
75550.e: Free space in the direction of their gaze stops the person looking cramped. The viewer follows their gaze into the picture.
75550.m: Leave more space in the direction the person is looking.

75551.q: In the golden ratio, roughly what percentage of a line does the larger part make up?
75551.e: In the golden ratio, the larger part is about 61.8 percent of the whole line. The smaller part is about 38.2 percent.
75551.m: In the golden ratio, the larger part is about 62 percent long.

75552.q: Why do artists often use the golden ratio when composing a picture?
75552.e: If you divide a picture by the golden ratio, it looks balanced but not boring. That is why important things are often not placed right in the middle.
75552.m: The golden ratio makes a picture look harmonious.

75553.q: Which number sequence is closely linked to the golden ratio, because the ratio of two neighbouring numbers gets closer and closer to it?
75553.e: In the Fibonacci sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, each number is the sum of the two before it. If you divide two neighbouring numbers, such as 13 by 8, the result gets close to 1.618.
75553.m: The Fibonacci sequence approaches the golden ratio.

75556.q: What do you call a rectangle whose long and short sides are in the golden ratio?
75556.e: In a golden rectangle, the long side is about 1.618 times as long as the short side. If you cut off a square, another golden rectangle is left over.
75556.m: A golden rectangle has sides in the golden ratio.

75557.q: Which famous architect was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1887?
75557.e: Le Corbusier's real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret. He designed a system of measurements based on the human body and the golden ratio, called the Modulor.
75557.m: Le Corbusier came from La Chaux-de-Fonds.

75558.q: What is the basic idea of the golden ratio?
a: Whole to larger part as larger to smaller part
Both parts are always exactly the same size
The small part is half the large part
The whole is three times as long as one part
75558.e: In the golden ratio, the whole line relates to the larger part in the same way as the larger part relates to the smaller one. Both ratios come to about 1.618.
75558.m: In the golden ratio, both ratios are equal.

75559.q: What is a single picture in a comic strip called?
75559.e: A comic is made up of many individual pictures called panels. Together they tell a story.
75559.m: A single comic picture is called a panel.

75560.q: How does a comic show that a character is only thinking something and not saying it?
a: With an arrow to the mouth
75560.e: Thoughts go in a thought bubble that looks like a cloud. Small circles lead from the bubble to the character's head.
75560.m: In comics, thoughts go in a cloud bubble.

75561.q: What do you call words like “Boing”, “Crash” or “Whoosh” that show sounds in a comic?
75561.e: Onomatopoeia imitates sounds with letters. In comics these words are often drawn big and colourful.
75561.m: Sound words in comics are called onomatopoeia.

75562.q: How does a comic show that a character is moving fast?
75562.e: Motion lines or speed lines are strokes behind the character. They show the direction and speed of a movement.
75562.m: Motion lines show speed in comics.

75563.q: What is the name of the young reporter from Belgium who has adventures with his white dog Snowy?
75563.e: Tintin and Snowy were created by the Belgian artist Hergé. The comics appeared from 1929 and were translated into many languages.
75563.m: Tintin and his dog Snowy are famous comic characters from Belgium.

75564.q: In which direction do you read a traditional Japanese manga?
75564.e: Japanese writing is traditionally read in vertical columns from right to left. That is why, for us, a manga starts “at the back”.
75564.m: You read a manga from right to left.

75565.q: When reading a comic, what do you fill in in your head in the white space between two pictures?
75565.e: Between two comic pictures, part of the story is often missing. The reader imagines what happens during that time.
75565.m: Between two comic pictures, you imagine the action.

75566.q: How does a comic usually show that a character is shouting loudly?
75566.e: A jagged speech bubble with big, bold letters stands for shouting. A dotted bubble, on the other hand, usually means whispering.
75566.m: A jagged speech bubble shows loud shouting.

75567.q: What does a still life show?
a: Objects that do not move, like fruit or jugs
Mountains and lakes in the evening light
75567.e: A still life shows lifeless things arranged by the artist. Fruit, flowers, glasses and jugs are typical.
75567.m: A still life shows lifeless objects.

75568.q: What is a still life called in French, which literally means “dead nature”?
75568.e: In French it is called “nature morte”, meaning dead nature. In German and English, on the other hand, it is called still life.
75568.m: In French, a still life is called “nature morte”.

75569.q: In which country was still life painting especially popular in the 17th century?
75569.e: In the 17th century, Dutch artists painted countless still lifes for wealthy citizens. This is known as the Golden Age of Dutch painting.
75569.m: In the 17th century, still life flourished in the Netherlands.

75570.q: What do you call a portrait that shows a person from the side?
75570.e: In profile, you see the face exactly from the side. Portraits like this are also familiar from coins.
75570.m: A portrait from the side is called a profile.

75571.q: What kind of picture is Rembrandt's famous “Night Watch”?
75571.e: The “Night Watch” shows a group of Amsterdam citizens from a civic guard company. Group portraits like this were popular in the Netherlands.
75571.m: The Night Watch is a group portrait.

75572.q: What do you call a portrait that shows a person from the head down to the chest?
75572.e: A bust portrait shows the head, shoulders and chest. A full-length figure, on the other hand, shows the whole body from head to toe.
75572.m: A bust portrait shows the person down to the chest.

75574.q: Which city full of canals did the Italian painter Canaletto paint especially often?
75574.e: In the 18th century, Canaletto painted very precise views of Venice. Pictures like these are called vedute.
75574.m: Canaletto painted precise views of Venice.

75575.q: Why do artists often paint tiny people next to the mountains in a picture of the Alps?
a: To make the mountains look enormous
To make the picture more colourful
To make the sky look brighter
75575.e: Next to small figures, you can see how huge glaciers and rocks are. The Aargau painter Caspar Wolf already used this trick in the 18th century.
75575.m: Small people make mountains look huge in a picture.

75576.q: Harald Naegeli became known in the late 1970s as the “Sprayer of Zurich”. What did he spray on house walls at night?
75576.e: Harald Naegeli sprayed delicate stick figures on walls in Zurich at night. He was convicted for it, but later also honoured as an artist.
75576.m: Harald Naegeli is known as the “Sprayer of Zurich”.

75577.q: What do you call the quickly sprayed signature or name abbreviation of a graffiti artist?
75577.e: A tag is a sprayer's personal signature. It is the simplest form of graffiti.
75577.m: A tag is a sprayer's signature.

75578.q: What do you call a large wall painting on the front of a building, often painted legally?
75578.e: The word mural comes from the Latin “murus” for wall. Murals often cover whole walls and are usually commissioned.
75578.m: A mural is a large wall painting.

75579.q: What is the street art form called where trees or railings are wrapped in knitting?
75579.e: In yarn bombing, also called urban knitting, objects in public spaces are covered with knitted wool. It can easily be removed again.
75579.m: In yarn bombing, the city is decorated with wool.

75580.q: What are posters or paper pictures called that are stuck onto walls with paste?
75580.e: Paste-ups are painted or printed at home and then stuck to the wall with paste. This way even large pictures can be put up quickly.
75580.m: Paste-ups are paper pictures stuck onto walls.

75581.q: Which New York artist drew figures in chalk on empty advertising spaces in the subway in the 1980s?
75581.e: Keith Haring drew with white chalk on black, empty poster spaces in the New York subway. His simple, lively figures became world-famous.
75581.m: Keith Haring drew chalk figures in the subway.

75582.q: What is the technique called where a picture is created by cleaning dirt off a wall?
75582.e: In reverse graffiti, nothing is sprayed on; instead, dirt is removed in a planned way. The picture is formed by the clean areas.
75582.m: Reverse graffiti is made by cleaning off dirt.

75583.q: What did Paul Klee discover for his art on his trip to Tunisia in 1914?
75583.e: The bright light in North Africa made a deep impression on Klee. He wrote in his diary that he and colour were now one.
75583.m: On his trip to Tunisia, Klee discovered colour.

75584.q: Which musical instrument did Paul Klee play very well?
75584.e: Paul Klee came from a family of musicians and was an excellent violinist. Music also influenced his pictures.
75584.m: Paul Klee was also a good violinist.

75585.q: What shape are the roofs of the Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern?
75585.e: The Zentrum Paul Klee opened in 2005. Its three wave-shaped roofs are reminiscent of a hilly landscape.
75585.m: The Zentrum Paul Klee has three wave-shaped roofs.

75586.q: Apart from people, what did the Swiss painter Ferdinand Hodler especially like to paint?
75586.e: Hodler often painted Swiss landscapes such as Lake Thun or the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau. Clear shapes and calm colours are typical.
75586.m: Ferdinand Hodler liked to paint mountains and lakes.

75587.q: What do Ferdinand Hodler's large murals in the Swiss National Museum in Zurich show?
75587.e: For the National Museum, Hodler painted the retreat of the Confederates from the Battle of Marignano in 1515. At the time the pictures caused heated debate.
75587.m: Hodler's murals in the National Museum show a battle of the Confederates.

75588.q: Which Swiss lake did Ferdinand Hodler paint especially often with the mountains in the background?
75588.e: Hodler painted Lake Thun with the Stockhorn range in many versions. He emphasised clear, horizontal bands of shore, water and mountains.

75589.q: What do you call art like Jean Tinguely's machines, where the work moves?
75589.e: The word kinetic comes from the Greek word for movement. Tinguely's sculptures made of scrap turn, clatter and rattle.
75589.m: Kinetic art is art in motion.

75590.q: What material did Jean Tinguely often use to build his machine sculptures?
75590.e: Tinguely collected wheels, iron parts and motors. From these he built sculptures that turn, clatter and rattle.
75590.m: Tinguely built his machines from scrap.

75591.q: On which river is the Museum Tinguely in Basel?
75591.e: The Museum Tinguely opened on the bank of the Rhine in Basel in 1996. It shows the largest collection of Tinguely's works.
75591.m: The Museum Tinguely is on the Rhine in Basel.

75692.q: What can you count on the cross-section of a tree trunk to estimate its age?
75692.e: A tree usually grows a new ring every year. If you count the growth rings, you know roughly how old the tree is.
75692.m: Each growth ring stands for about one year.

75693.q: What do you call a flat, long piece of wood that you can use to build a shelf, for example?
75693.e: Flat, long planks are sawn from a tree trunk. They are used to build shelves, boxes or floors.
75693.m: A plank is a flat piece of wood.

75694.q: What happens to wood when it falls into water?
75694.e: Most kinds of wood are lighter than water, so they float on top. That is why rafts and boats used to be made of wood.
75694.m: Most kinds of wood float on water.

75695.q: What do you use to make a rough wooden edge smooth?
75695.e: Sandpaper is coated with fine, hard grains. If you rub it over the wood, the surface becomes smooth.

75696.q: What is a small, sharp piece of wood called that can stick into your skin?
75696.e: A splinter is a thin sliver of wood that can dig into your skin. That is why wooden edges are sanded smooth.
75696.m: A splinter is a small sliver of wood.

75697.q: What is the outer protective layer of a tree trunk?
75697.e: Bark wraps around the trunk like a skin. It protects the tree from cold, animals and diseases.

75698.q: What is the dark, round spot in a plank called, where a branch once grew out of the trunk?
75698.e: Where a branch grew out of the trunk, you can see a round, often dark spot in the plank. This spot is called a knot.
75698.m: A knot in a plank shows where a branch once grew.

75699.q: What do you call the lines in the wood that you can see on a plank?
75699.e: The grain comes from the growth rings and the wood fibres. That is why every plank has its own pattern.
75699.m: The grain is the natural pattern in wood.

75700.q: What is paper mostly made from today?
75700.e: To make paper, wood fibres are mixed with lots of water into a pulp. Thin sheets are then pressed and dried from it.
75700.m: Paper is mostly made from wood fibres.

75701.e: Waste paper is paper that has already been used. You bundle it up and hand it in for collection so that new paper can be made from it.
75701.m: New paper can be made from waste paper.

75702.q: What is the Japanese art of folding figures out of paper called?
75702.e: Origami comes from Japan and means paper folding. You fold animals, flowers or boats without scissors or glue.
75702.m: Origami is the art of paper folding.

75703.q: What happens to paper when it gets wet?
a: It goes soft and tears easily
75703.e: Water gets in between the fibres of the paper. As a result the fibres hold together less well and the paper tears easily.

75704.q: What do you call paper that is dyed and used for craft work?
75704.e: Coloured paper comes in many colours. You cut and glue it for pictures, cards and decorations.
75704.m: Coloured paper comes in many colours for crafts.

75705.q: What is the craft material made of soaked paper and glue that becomes hard when it dries?
75705.e: For papier-mâché, you stick strips of paper in layers onto a shape, for example a balloon. When it dries, everything becomes firm.
75705.m: You can make papier-mâché from paper and glue.

75706.q: Which paper is see-through enough to trace a picture underneath?
75706.e: Tracing paper lets a lot of light through. That is why you can see a picture underneath and draw over it with a pencil.
75706.m: You can trace pictures with tracing paper.

75707.q: What is cardboard like compared with normal paper?
75707.e: Like paper, cardboard is made of fibres, but it is much thicker. That is why it is stiff and good for boxes.
75707.m: Cardboard is thicker and firmer than paper.

75708.q: What is cardboard with a wavy layer in the middle called?
75708.e: Corrugated cardboard has a wavy paper layer inside between two smooth layers. This makes it light but still strong.
75708.m: Corrugated cardboard has a wavy layer inside.

75709.q: What is often made from corrugated cardboard?
75709.e: Corrugated cardboard is light and strong. That is why it is used for boxes for parcels and for moving house.
75709.m: Boxes for parcels are often made of corrugated cardboard.

75710.q: What helps cardboard fold nice and straight?
75710.e: If you score the fold line along a ruler with a bone folder or a blunt point, the cardboard bends exactly there. This makes the edge nice and straight.
75710.m: A scored line makes folding cardboard easier.

a: Soft earth that you can shape
75711.e: Clay is a fine earth from nature. With water it becomes soft and you can knead and shape it.
75711.m: Clay is an earth you can shape.

75712.q: What do you have to do with a clay figure to make it really hard?
75712.e: Dried clay breaks easily and goes soft again in water. Only at very high heat, much hotter than in a kitchen, does it become hard as stone.
75712.m: Clay only becomes really hard when it is fired.

75713.q: What is the special oven called in which clay is fired?
75713.e: A kiln gets much hotter than a kitchen oven. This great heat makes the clay hard.
75713.m: Clay is fired in a kiln.

75714.q: What happens to clay if it is left in the air for a long time?
a: It always stays just as soft
75714.e: Clay contains water. In the air the water evaporates and the clay becomes dry and firm. That is why clay is covered with a damp cloth or plastic.
75714.m: Clay dries out in the air.

75715.q: What do you call a thick roll of clay used to build up a pot layer by layer?
75715.e: In the coil technique, you roll clay into long sausages. You lay them in rings on top of each other and smooth them together well.
75715.m: You can build pots with clay coils.

75716.q: On which spinning disc do you shape bowls out of clay?
75716.e: On the potter's wheel, the clay spins quickly round and round. With wet hands you shape it into round pots.
75716.m: On a potter's wheel, the clay spins round.

75717.q: What is the shiny, glass-like coating on clay crockery called?
75717.e: The glaze is applied before the second firing. In the heat it melts into a smooth, often coloured layer.

75718.q: What do you call someone who makes pots and bowls out of clay?
75718.e: Potters shape pots, plates and cups out of clay. Today the job is often called ceramicist.
75718.m: A potter makes pots out of clay.

75719.q: Which animal does most wool come from?
75719.e: Sheep have a thick, curly coat. It is sheared off and made into wool.

75720.q: How do you make a long thread from loose wool?
75720.e: When spinning, the wool fibres are pulled and twisted. This creates a strong, long thread.

75721.q: What is a wound-up piece of wool thread called?
75721.e: Wool is often bought as a ball. The thread is wound up in a round shape and is easy to unwind.
75721.m: A ball of wool is wool that has been wound up.

75722.q: Which tool with a small hook at the tip do you need for crocheting?
75722.e: The crochet hook has a small hook at the front. You use it to pull the wool through loops and crochet a pot holder, for example.
75722.m: You need a crochet hook to crochet.

75723.q: What is a single loop in knitting called?
75723.e: A piece of knitting is made of many stitches. Each stitch is a small loop of yarn.
75723.m: Knitting is made of many stitches.

75724.q: What do you get if you rub wool with warm soapy water?
75724.e: Warmth, soap and rubbing make the wool fibres hook firmly into each other. This creates a dense fabric called felt.
75724.m: Wool, soapy water and rubbing make felt.

75725.q: What are woollen clothes especially good for?
75725.e: Lots of air is trapped between the crinkly wool fibres. This air holds in your body heat.
75725.m: Wool keeps you nice and warm.

75726.q: Where do the soft fibres of cotton grow?
a: In the seed pods of a plant
75726.e: The cotton plant forms pods with white, fluffy fibres. These fibres are spun into yarn for fabrics.
75726.m: Cotton comes from the cotton plant.

75727.q: Which animal makes the threads for silk?
75727.e: The caterpillar of the silk moth spins itself into a cocoon made of one long, fine thread. Silk is made from these threads.

75728.q: Which plant is linen made from?
75728.e: Flax has long fibres in its stem. These are woven into the cool fabric linen.

a: A template for cutting out fabric
75729.e: A sewing pattern shows the shape of the fabric pieces. You lay it on the fabric, trace round it and cut out the pieces.
75729.m: A sewing pattern helps you cut out fabric.

75730.q: Which side of the fabric do you see when you wear a piece of clothing normally?
75730.e: On fabric, the nice outer side is called the right side. The inner side is called the wrong side.
75730.m: The nice side of a fabric is called the right side.

75731.q: What often happens to a woollen jumper if you wash it too hot?
75731.e: Heat and movement make the wool fibres felt together. The jumper contracts and gets smaller.
75731.m: Wool can shrink in a hot wash.

75732.q: What is a small piece of fabric called that you sew over a hole in your trousers?
75732.e: You cover a hole with a patch. You sew it on or iron it on, so you can keep wearing the trousers.
75732.m: You mend a hole with a patch.

75733.q: How do you carry scissors safely?
75733.e: You hold the scissors closed with the point facing down. That way you will not hurt anyone if you trip.
75733.m: Carry scissors closed with the point down.

75734.q: How do you pass scissors to someone correctly?
75734.e: You hold the scissors by the closed blades and offer the other person the handle. That way nobody can cut themselves.

75735.q: How many blades does a normal pair of scissors have?
75735.e: Scissors have two blades that slide past each other. The paper or fabric is cut between them.

75736.q: Why shouldn't you cut paper with fabric scissors?
75736.e: Paper contains tiny hard particles that wear down the sharp blades. Blunt fabric scissors no longer cut fabric cleanly.
75736.m: Only cut fabric with fabric scissors.

75737.q: What helps when cutting a curve with scissors?
75737.e: For a curve, the scissors stay still and you turn the paper with your other hand. This makes the line nice and round.
75737.m: For curves, turn the paper, not the scissors.

75738.q: Which scissors cut a zigzag edge into fabric?
75738.e: Pinking shears have jagged blades. The zigzag edge stops the fabric fraying so quickly at the edge.
75738.m: Pinking shears cut a zigzag edge.

75739.q: Which scissors with rounded tips are meant for children doing crafts?
75739.e: Craft scissors have rounded tips. That way you are less likely to prick yourself when cutting paper.
75739.m: Children cut paper with craft scissors.

75740.q: Which glue is good for sticking wood?
75740.e: PVA glue is white but turns clear as it dries. It sticks pieces of wood together very firmly.
75740.m: Wood sticks well with PVA glue.

75741.q: What must you do after joining two pieces of wood with glue?
a: Press them firmly and let them dry
Paint them while the glue is wet
75741.e: Glue needs time to dry. If you press the pieces firmly together and leave them alone, the joint holds better.
75741.m: Glued pieces must be pressed together and left to dry.

75742.q: Which glue comes in a small stick that you twist up like a lipstick?
75742.e: You twist the glue stick up and rub it over the paper. It is clean and good for paper crafts.
75742.m: A glue stick is good for paper.

75743.q: What is a glue called that you can mix from flour and water?
75743.e: Flour and water together make a sticky mixture. This paste is used for paper crafts or wallpaper, for example.
75743.m: You can make paste from flour and water.

75744.q: What is especially dangerous about a hot glue gun?
75744.e: A glue stick is melted inside the hot glue gun. The liquid glue is so hot that you can burn yourself on it.
75744.m: Hot glue can burn your skin.

75745.q: Why should you only put on a little glue?
a: Too much glue oozes out and dries slowly
Too much glue turns the wood red
Too much glue makes the wood melt
Too much glue makes the wood lighter
75745.e: A thin layer of glue is enough. Too much glue oozes out at the edges, leaves marks and takes longer to dry.
75745.m: A thin layer of glue is enough.

a: A strip with a sticky side
75746.e: Sticky tape is a thin strip coated with glue on one side. You can tear it off and stick it on straight away.
75746.m: Sticky tape is sticky on one side.

75747.q: What does a saw have so that it can cut wood?
75747.e: The saw blade has lots of small, sharp teeth. As it moves back and forth, they remove the wood bit by bit.
75747.m: A saw cuts with its teeth.

75748.q: What is the fine wood powder called that is made when sawing?
75748.e: The teeth of the saw tear out tiny bits of wood. These fall down as fine sawdust.

75749.q: What do you use to hold the wood firmly while sawing?
75749.e: The wood must be held tightly while sawing, for example with a clamp or in a vice. Otherwise it slips and you can hurt yourself.
75749.m: When sawing, the wood must be clamped tight.

75750.q: Which saw can you use to cut fine curves out of thin wood?
75750.e: A fretsaw has a very thin blade. You can use it to cut curves and shapes out of thin plywood.
75750.m: You cut fine curves with a fretsaw.

75752.q: Why should you wear safety goggles when sawing?
a: So that no bits of wood fly into your eyes
So that the wood looks nicer
So that the saw is quieter
75752.e: When sawing, small bits of wood can fly around. Safety goggles protect your eyes from them.
75752.m: Safety goggles protect your eyes in the workshop.

75753.q: What do you draw on the wood before you saw?
75753.e: With a pencil and ruler you mark exactly where to saw. This makes the cut straight and in the right place.
75753.m: Before sawing, you mark the line.

75754.q: What do you usually need a hammer for?
75754.e: You use a hammer to knock nails into wood. While doing so, you take good care of your fingers.
75754.m: You knock in nails with a hammer.

75755.q: What are the two main parts of a hammer?
75755.e: A hammer has a heavy metal head and a handle to hold it by. The handle is often made of wood.
75755.m: A hammer has a head and a handle.

75756.q: What is the split, curved part of a claw hammer for?
75756.e: On a claw hammer, one side of the head is split. You can use it to grip a bent nail and pull it out.
75756.m: You pull out nails with the claw.

75757.q: Which hammer has a head made of rubber or wood so that it does not scratch anything?
75757.e: A soft hammer made of wood or rubber knocks parts together without making dents. You need it, for example, when fitting wooden parts together.
75757.m: A rubber mallet leaves no dents.

75758.q: What are nails usually made of?
75758.e: Nails are usually made of steel, which is a metal. That is why they are hard enough to go into wood.
75758.m: Nails are usually made of metal.

75759.q: What is the wide, flat end of a nail that you hit called?
75759.e: A nail has a flat head at the top and a point at the bottom. You hit the head with the hammer.
75759.m: You hit the head of the nail with the hammer.

75760.q: How do you start knocking in a nail?
a: Hold the nail with two fingers and tap lightly
Hold the nail with two fingers and hit hard straight away
Let go of the nail and hit hard straight away
Hold the nail in your fist and hit hard
75760.e: At first you hold the nail between your thumb and index finger and tap very lightly. As soon as it is firmly in, you take your fingers away and hit harder.
75760.m: First tap lightly, then hit harder.

75761.q: What often happens if you knock a nail in too close to the edge of a plank?
75761.e: The nail pushes the wood fibres apart. If there is too little wood at the edge, the plank splits.
75761.m: Do not knock nails in too close to the edge.

75762.q: What is the small hole in a sewing needle called, through which you thread the cotton?
75762.e: A sewing needle has a point at one end and a small hole at the other. This hole is called the eye.
75762.m: The thread goes through the eye of the needle.

75763.q: What protects your finger from the needle when sewing by hand?
75763.e: You put the thimble on your middle finger. With it you can push the needle through the fabric without pricking yourself.
75763.m: A thimble protects your finger when sewing.

75764.q: What do you put at the end of the thread so that it does not slip through the fabric?
75764.e: A knot at the end of the thread is thicker than the hole in the fabric. That way the thread stays caught at the first stitch.
75764.m: A knot holds the thread in the fabric.

75765.q: What is the line called where two pieces of fabric are sewn together?
75765.e: Where two pieces of fabric are joined with stitches, a seam is formed. On clothes you can see seams at the sides, for example.
75765.m: A seam joins two pieces of fabric.

75766.q: What is the simple stitch called where the needle keeps going up and down through the fabric?
75766.e: With running stitch, you stitch up and down at equal distances. This makes a dashed line.
75766.m: Running stitch is a simple up-and-down stitch.
